title: Who is asking?
brief: Every access decision needs two inputs: who the caller is and which groups they hold when the query runs. Decide how you get them, how fresh they must be and which identity the retriever runs as, while group counts, nesting and revocation speed are still open.

blocks.text: Identity is an input to every query

blocks.md:
The retriever must see the caller, not a service account. With the on-behalf-of (OBO) flow a middle tier exchanges the caller's access token for a downstream token using **delegated scopes only**, so roles stay with the user. If the downstream API enforces Conditional Access such as MFA, the middle tier must return 401 with a `WWW-Authenticate` header so the client can satisfy the challenge. A single-page app sends its access token to a middle-tier confidential client that runs OBO [[r25]].

The alternative is a **confused deputy**: one service identity with broad read access that filters in code. Every bug in that code becomes a leak, and the store cannot tell who asked. Azure's multitenant RAG guidance adds two rules: put an API layer in front of the stores so no other code can query them, and apply the filters on every retrieval, including those made inside an agent loop. Derive tenant and filters from the authenticated request, never from fields the client sends [[r22]].

blocks.title: Ways to resolve the caller's principals
blocks.intro: Each option trades freshness, latency and who owns the code. Whatever you pick, its cache or token lifetime is part of your revocation SLA.

options.name: Read the `groups` claim
options.summary: Use the list embedded in the access token.
cons: Capped at 200 groups for JWT, 150 for SAML and 6 for implicit flow
Membership is frozen until the token is refreshed
options.bestWhen: Users hold well under 200 groups and a token-lifetime delay is inside the revocation SLA.
options.avoidWhen: Users have many or nested groups, or revocation must take minutes.

options.name: Call Graph `transitiveMemberOf` per request
options.summary: Ask Microsoft Graph for direct and nested memberships.
cons: Extra round trip and Graph call volume
Page size is 100 by default, 999 at most
options.bestWhen: Overage or nested groups with moderate traffic, or behind a short cache.
options.avoidWhen: High request rates with no cache, or when a Graph outage must not block answers.

options.name: Cache memberships with a TTL
options.summary: Resolve once, reuse for a short time.
cons: The TTL becomes part of the revocation SLA
Stale after offboarding until it expires
options.bestWhen: Request rates are high and the TTL is well below the revocation SLA.
options.avoidWhen: Revocation must take effect in seconds.

options.name: Authorize on app roles
options.summary: Assign users and groups to app roles and read role names from the token.
pros: Code reads role names, not group ids
cons: Coarse: a few tiers, not per-document ACLs
options.bestWhen: Access has a few tiers such as reader, analyst and admin.
options.avoidWhen: ACLs are per team, per project or per document.

options.name: Let the search service expand groups from the user token
options.summary: Azure AI Search native ACLs match the token's user and group ids, resolving groups through Graph at query time.
pros: Fails closed if Graph is unavailable
cons: The first ACL query can be slower
options.bestWhen: Content already carries Entra object ids and you can accept preview.
options.avoidWhen: GA only is mandatory, or identities live outside Entra.

options.name: Call an internal entitlement service
options.summary: One service answers can-this-user-see-this for every source.
pros: Covers non-Entra identities and deny rules
cons: Must stay consistent with each source system
options.bestWhen: Identities or rules exist that no directory models.
options.avoidWhen: Everything already lives in Entra and the sources enforce their own rules.

steps.title: Validate the token
steps.md: Check signature, audience and expiry. Take `oid` from the token, never from the request body.

steps.title: Use the claim if present
steps.md: If a `groups` claim exists, use it as the principal set.

steps.title: Detect overage
steps.md: No claim? Check `hasgroups` (implicit flow) or `_claim_names` containing `groups`. Rely on the indicator, not on the `_claim_sources` endpoint, which may still name the legacy AAD Graph [[r23]].

steps.title: Call Graph
steps.md: `GET /users/{id}/transitiveMemberOf` with `$top=999`, following paging. Advanced queries such as `$count` need `ConsistencyLevel: eventual` and read an index that might lag [[r24]].

steps.title: Fail closed
steps.md: If groups cannot be resolved, return public documents only or an error, never unfiltered results.

blocks.caption: Least-privilege retrieval identities for Azure AI Search native ACLs. Preview as of 2026-10-13.

items.symptom: Users with many memberships get empty results, or see everything.
items.cause: Overage not handled. The claim is missing and the code treats no groups as no filter, or swallows the error.
items.fix: Detect `hasgroups` or `_claim_names`, call Graph and fail closed when groups cannot be resolved.

items.symptom: A user removed from a group still gets restricted answers for an hour.
items.cause: Memberships cached with a long TTL, or the token still carries the old claim until it refreshes.
items.fix: Count TTL and token lifetime inside the revocation SLA, shorten them for restricted tiers and re-check the top hits at the source.

items.symptom: Every user gets broad answers in staging and the tests pass.
items.cause: The retriever runs with an app-only token, a confused deputy, so the store never sees the user.
items.fix: Use OBO or token-based enforcement and add a test with two users who hold different access.

items.symptom: Filters match nothing for some users.
items.cause: ACL fields hold UPNs or emails while the code filters on object ids. Native ACL fields expect Entra object ids [[r15]].
items.fix: Store object ids (GUIDs) and filter on `oid` and group ids.

blocks.title: What interviewers listen for
blocks.md: Say where the user identity enters the system and which component could widen it. Candidates who skip overage either fail closed on heavy users or fail open on them. Also say how you debug: elevated read is an explicit admin request on Search POST (REST `2026-05-01-preview` or later), not the app's normal path [[r12]].

quiz.q: Once nesting is expanded, a user belongs to 2,300 groups. You call `transitiveMemberOf` with the maximum page size of 999. What is the minimum number of requests?
quiz.explain: 2,300 divided by 999 is 2.3, so you need 3 pages. At the default page size of 100 it would take 23 requests, which is why you page at the maximum and cache the result for a TTL below your revocation SLA.

quiz.q: Users in many groups see no restricted results. The code reads `claims["groups"]` and falls back to an empty list. What explains it?
options: The access token has expired and the service silently returns public results
The user lacks the Search Index Data Reader role on the index
Group overage: the code never calls Graph
Entra emits group claims only in SAML tokens, never in JWTs
quiz.explain: `_claim_names` containing `groups` is the overage indicator, so the list is not in the token. The fix is to call Graph `transitiveMemberOf`, not the legacy endpoint in `_claim_sources`. An expired token would fail validation, a missing role would fail the call rather than shrink results, and JWTs also carry groups up to the 200 limit.

quiz.q: Select every statement that is true about the on-behalf-of flow.
options: The middle tier uses delegated scopes, so roles stay with the user.
It lets the middle tier reuse its own app roles so the downstream API sees a trusted service.
If the downstream API requires MFA through Conditional Access, the middle tier returns 401 with a `WWW-Authenticate` header so the client can satisfy it.
A single-page app should send its access token to a middle-tier confidential client to run OBO.
It removes the need for the downstream store to check permissions.
quiz.explain: OBO keeps the user as the subject with delegated scopes, surfaces Conditional Access challenges through 401 and WWW-Authenticate, and runs in a confidential middle tier. Reusing app roles is the confused-deputy shape OBO avoids, and the downstream store still enforces its own permissions for the user it sees.

quiz.q: Users hold up to 400 nested groups, a removed membership must stop working within about 5 minutes, and traffic is 50 requests per second. Which resolution strategy fits best?
options: Read the groups claim and accept whatever freshness the token lifetime gives
Call Graph `transitiveMemberOf` on every request without any cache
Authorize on app roles only and drop the group ACLs
quiz.explain: A 2 minute TTL keeps the cache inside the 5 minute target and removes most Graph calls at 50 requests per second. The claim is capped at 200 groups and frozen until the token refreshes, a Graph call on every request adds a round trip and call volume you do not need, and app roles are too coarse for per-team ACLs.

takeaways: Pass the user's token downstream with OBO so the store sees the user, not a broad service account.
Handle group overage every time: 200 groups for JWT, 150 for SAML, then call Graph.
Cache TTLs and token lifetimes are part of the revocation SLA. State them.
Use separate identities for ingest, query, the caller and break-glass debugging.
On any resolution error, fail closed.
